betterCitation: Rosa Luxemburg, The Russian Revolution, ch. 6, The Problem of Dictatorship: her marginal note (trans. Bertram D. Wolfe, 1940)
reason: The wording survives and the provenance does not. The Wolfe text as the Marxists Internet Archive transcribes it does read, in the body of chapter 6: Freedom only for the supporters of the government, only for the members of one party, however numerous they may be, is no freedom at all. Freedom is always and exclusively freedom for the one who thinks differently. Not because of any fanatical concept of justice but because all that is instructive, wholesome and purifying in political freedom depends on this essential characteristic. So the proposed sentence exists in the named translation, the chapter is the sixth in that archive contents list, and it is titled The Problem of Dictatorship; the archive header names Workers Age Publishers, New York, 1940, and Bertram Wolfe as translator, matching the edition line. What breaks the card is what it does not say, and what the evidence positively asserts. The evidence says the sentence stands in the main text. In the manuscript it does not. Luxemburg wrote it as a Randbemerkung, a marginal note beside the main text, and she wrote it in the fourth chapter, not the sixth; the German article on the sentence states this and cites a facsimile of the original hand. Worse for the locator: that marginal note is not in Paul Levi first publication of the manuscript in 1922, the printing every later edition descends from, and it entered print only in a later edition, probably the first complete Paris edition of 1938. A reader who checks the cited chapter against Levi 1922 or against the chapter divisions of the German text will not find the line where the card sends them, because chapter 6 is Wolfe editorial division and not Luxemburg. Three further things are unproved, and the standard here is that a confident citation is worse than an honest hedge. The 1940 Workers Age pamphlet itself has not been seen; only the archive transcription and its header claim have been seen, and since the sentence was absent from the 1922 German text the whole chain into a 1940 English pamphlet rests on that single header. The Russian Revolution is an unfinished manuscript written in Breslau prison in 1918 and published after her death, which a card naming it flatly as a work does not tell the reader. And the note field is empty, so none of this reaches the page. The line is worth keeping and can ship corrected: take the better source line above, which runs to 125 characters, leads with the name, carries no dash and says plainly that the sentence is her marginal note; give it a note saying the manuscript was written in prison in 1918 and left unfinished, that Luxemburg wrote this sentence in the margin beside the main text, that it is absent from the Levi printing of 1922 and first appears in a later edition, and that Wolfe sets it in the main text of his chapter 6. Cap and scope are clean either way: shipped.js gives rosa luxemburg at 1 of 3, from month 2, not banned, nothing shipped and no near opening; 1918 and 1940 are both well before 2000; the sentence needs no warning and is a true September line about what is owed to the person who disagrees.
